item.dc:creator: Christoph Schwab, Josephine Westermann, Jakob Zech

item.title: Recalibrating Many Questions with Few Labels: Minimax Rates and Identification Limits
item.description: arXiv:2610.18488v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many related prediction problems, which we call questions, come with few labels each. What information can be shared across them, and what is actually necessary for good decisions? We answer both for recalibration, motivated by decision models such as Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) that return a probability for any yes/no question a developer writes. A predictor reports a probability $P$ with output law $\mu$ on $m$ questions, each with $n$ labels and a nondecreasing map $g_j(p)=\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid P=p)$; the compound risk is the excess Brier score over the true maps, averaged over questions. Over maps within sup-distance $\tau\le 1$ and total variation $V\le 2$ of one nondecreasing shape (fixed effects), the minimax compound risk is $(mn)^{-2/3}+\min\{\tau^2,1/n\}+\min\{\tau^2,V^2,(V/n)^{2/3}\}$ up to universal constants, for every non-atomic $\mu$. A pooled isotonic fit with a per-question correction sized once, on held-out labels of all questions, attains it without knowing $\tau$, $V$ or $\mu$ ($n\ge 2$, $m\ge 3$); tuning each question on its own labels loses a factor of order $\min\{n,\log(m^2/n)\}$ when the maps differ by constants and $m^2/n$ is large. When the maps are drawn from an unknown prior (random effects), other questions need not identify the Bayes rule. The loss, the identification regret, is at most $2^{-n}$ once the law of a question's data is known, extending a bound of Skibinsky (1968) for coins, and in the worst case at least $\beta_\star^{-n}/(72\sqrt{n})$ at every finite $m$, where $\beta_\star\approx 3.583$. Beyond a few labels per question, what cannot be learned is nearly unnecessary. For constant maps (an uninformative predictor) and constant-map priors, the exponential base is exactly $\beta_\star$, not the 4 suggested by the moment range; for monotone maps it lies in $[2,\beta_\star]$.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Li, Chiwun Yang

item.title: Two For The Price Of One: Curvature-Aware Pruning Preserves Influence Functions Too
item.description: arXiv:2610.18516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Post-training pruning enables efficient deployment, but conventional methods do not explicitly preserve internal-gradient alignment between sparse and dense models. We study novel connections between downstream performance of compressed models and the ability to retain gradient information via influence-function preservation. Central to this connection is a curvature-aware objective that accounts for both layer activations and backpropagated gradients. Despite its promise, this objective remains underexplored in pruning due to a lack of efficient solvers. We introduce $\texttt{CACTUS}$, a novel ADMM-based optimizer supporting both pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions of pre-trained weights. Compared to LLM-Surgeon which targets the same objective, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ can achieve over an order-of-magnitude speedup. At $50\%$ pruning of Qwen3-4B, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ reduces the C4 perplexity gap to the dense model by $45\%$, improves compressed-to-dense per-sample gradient cosine similarity on WikiText-2 from $0.670$ to $0.755$, and runs over $28\times$ faster than LLM-Surgeon on substantially weaker hardware. By preserving influence functions, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ supports effective data selection. On Llama-3.2-3B, fine-tuning a fresh dense model on the $5\%$ of data selected by $\texttt{CACTUS}$ achieves $49.44\%$ accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard, compared with $47.22\%$ using ALPS and $49.54\%$ using dense-model selection. Finally, integrating $\texttt{CACTUS}$ with LoGRA, a recent gradient-projection strategy, on Qwen3-4B with MLP layers pruned to 2:4 sparsity and a rank-64 correction retains a $0.711$ cosine alignment with dense LoGRA-projected C4 gradients.
item.dc:creator: Mehdi Makni, Natalia Ponomareva, Rahul Mazumder

item.title: Minimax rates for pointwise CATE estimation: the role of design smoothness
item.description: arXiv:2610.18623v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the role of design smoothness in the minimax estimation of conditional average treatment effects at a fixed covariate point. For design densities bounded above and away from zero, without further regularity, we derive upper and lower risk bounds with an arbitrarily small gap in the convergence-rate exponent. Under uniform design, we obtain matching upper and lower bounds at interior points in the regime of low nuisance smoothness. These results show that rough covariate designs can lead to slower rates than uniform designs, even under the same smoothness assumptions on the treatment effect and nuisance functions, highlighting the role of the covariate distribution in pointwise causal estimation.
item.dc:creator: Yuxuan Hou, Zhenghan Li

item.title: BridgeTwist: Twisting Schr\"odinger Bridges for Training-Free Conditional Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.18658v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative models are often required to serve many downstream conditional tasks. In the training-free setting, a pretrained unconditional model is reused as a prior and combined with a task-specific likelihood to sample from the corresponding posterior. While such training-free samplers have been developed for diffusion and flow models, their counterpart for Schr\"odinger bridge (SB) models remains unexplored, despite the growing appeal of SBs as flexible stochastic transport models between general source and target distributions. We propose BridgeTwist, a training-free conditional sampler for pretrained SB generative models, formulated as a tempered twisted sequential Monte Carlo scheme. Its twist is a closed-form plug-in surrogate, obtained by combining the velocity and score fields exposed by SB pretraining into an endpoint predictor and evaluating the likelihood there. Since this surrogate is less reliable near the source, we temper the twist with a time-varying exponent, downweighting its influence at early steps. We further introduce a bridge-shaped inference-time diffusion schedule that concentrates the proposal noise in the interior of the path. Telescoping importance weights then cancel all intermediate twist factors, yielding an asymptotically exact sampler for the posterior. Empirically, BridgeTwist outperforms training-free baselines on class-conditional and text-prompted image generation, and is competitive with specialized inverse problem solvers on inpainting, deblurring, and super-resolution.
item.dc:creator: Mengyu Li, Qianqian Qu, Jun S. Liu

item.title: From Fourier Amplitudes to Persistence Images for Impact-Echo Defect Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.18732v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Impact-echo testing is a nondestructive testing method used to detect internal defects in concrete structures. However, boundary reflections, structured interference, and measurement noise can produce complex Fourier amplitude spectra, making defect classification difficult. We constructed a two-dimensional frequency--amplitude persistence image (FA-PI) from the Fourier amplitude spectrum. Using a fixed parameterization of exact multi-parameter persistent homology, each retained Fourier component is represented with frequency-bin location as one coordinate and amplitude as the other, and Gaussian kernels are then applied in this two-dimensional space. This construction has a direct analytical connection to the corresponding one-dimensional Gaussian-smoothed Fourier amplitude spectrum. FA-PI was evaluated on an experimental backfill-void dataset and a public bridge-deck impact-echo dataset, and compared with raw and Gaussian-smoothed Fourier amplitude spectra using a linear classifier with a Softmax output and identical signal-level data splits. The evaluation included original signals and signals corrupted by Gaussian noise, sinusoidal interference, or mixed noise, with matching noise types and signal-to-noise ratios during training, validation, and testing. Performance was assessed using accuracy and macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score. Across the two datasets, FA-PI consistently outperformed the raw and Gaussian-smoothed Fourier baselines in the noisy-condition summaries. These findings indicate that representing Fourier spectral components in a two-dimensional frequency--amplitude space can improve impact-echo defect classification beyond frequency-axis smoothing alone.
item.dc:creator: Keunsu Kim, Suyoung Choi, Meiyan Kang

item.title: A Rate Transfer Method: Convergence Rates in Stochastic Gradient Descent via Stochastic Calculus
item.description: arXiv:2610.18739v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a rate-transfer method that converts finite-time Lyapunov estimates for an associated stochastic differential equation (SDE) into finite-time convergence bounds for stochastic gradient algorithms. Under generic moment and smoothness conditions, the convergence analysis of the stochastic gradient method reduces to a calculus argument verifying a Lyapunov generator inequality for the SDE. The method recovers established rates for classical stochastic gradient methods and provides a way to establish convergence rates for new optimization algorithms through calculus arguments applied to their associated SDEs.
item.dc:creator: Neil Walton

item.title: Designing for Prediction: Planning Formulas for Expected Out-of-Sample $R^2$ and $r$
item.description: arXiv:2610.18781v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Design calculations let researchers gauge, before data is collected, whether a planned study is likely to detect an effect. In this paper, we develop such calculations for predictive models using ordinary least squares and ridge regression under leave-one-out cross-validation. To do so, we derive closed-form expressions relating the expected out-of-sample $R^2$ and the expected correlation between observed and predicted outcomes to four design-stage quantities: sample size, number of predictors, an assumed population $R^2$ ($\rho^2_{in}$) and a design efficiency factor $D^*$ (which summarizes how leverage is distributed across observations). Unlike the classical shrinkage formulas, which depend only on sample size and dimension, these are sensitive to how covariates are arranged -- to imbalance and skew. A simulation study assesses the accuracy of the formulas against realized values under a variety of data generating mechanisms. We apply the methods to a published study predicting personality from smartphone behavior and show that the design formulas would have indicated, before any analyses were run, that least squares could not be expected to beat the sample mean while ridge could. An R package, predpower, implements the calculations.
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Tipton

item.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Thompson Sampling for Multi-Armed Bandits
item.description: arXiv:1808.02932v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In stochastic multi-armed bandits, rewards are generated by an unknown distribution; the world's reward uncertainty induces the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Thompson sampling (TS) addresses this trade-off elegantly, but requires knowing the reward model's parametric form to sample from its posterior and compute per-arm expected rewards ---which limits its applicability as it demands per-scenario model specification and hyperparameter tuning. We here adopt Bayesian nonparametric (BNP) mixture models to remove this requirement, extending TS to arbitrary reward distributions. We model each arm's unknown reward distribution with an independent BNP Gaussian mixture, which can approximate any continuous reward density, and adapts its complexity to sequentially observed data. Embedding the BNP mixture model into TS yields Nonparametric TS, an algorithm that sequentially learns the reward model that best approximates the true, yet unknown, per-arm reward distribution, avoiding case-by-case model specification and hyperparameter tuning. We empirically demonstrate that ($i$) Nonparametric TS matches the regret performance of Oracle TS policies that know the true reward model; ($ii$) it favorably compares (in cumulative regret and volatility) to a suite of state-of-the-art alternatives across multimodal, outlier-contaminated, and non-exponential-family reward distributions; and ($iii$) its Bayesian nonparametric inference remains computationally practical and accurate for regret minimization.
item.dc:creator: I\~nigo Urteaga, Chris H. Wiggins

item.title: Equilibrium Distribution for t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding with Generalized Kernels
item.description: arXiv:2505.24311v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We extend the results by Auffinger and Fletcher in 2023 on the large-sample limit of t-SNE to a broader class of input and output kernels. We prove that under natural assumptions on the input distribution and the decay of the output kernel, if perplexity scales linearly with data size, the empirical measures and values of minimizers converge to an equilibrium distribution. We conclude with numerical examples comparing different kernels.
item.dc:creator: Yi Gu, Antonio Auffinger

item.title: High-Order Error Bounds for Markovian LSA with Richardson-Romberg Extrapolation
item.description: arXiv:2508.05570v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we study the bias and high-order error bounds of the Linear Stochastic Approximation (LSA) algorithm with Polyak-Ruppert (PR) averaging under Markovian noise. We focus on the version of the algorithm with constant step size $\alpha$ and propose a novel decomposition of the bias via a linearization technique. We analyze the structure of the bias and show that the leading-order term is linear in $\alpha$ and cannot be eliminated by PR averaging. To address this, we apply the Richardson-Romberg (RR) extrapolation procedure, which effectively cancels the leading bias term. We derive high-order moment bounds for the RR iterates and show that the leading error term aligns with the asymptotically optimal covariance matrix of the vanilla averaged LSA iterates.
item.dc:creator: Ilya Levin, Alexey Naumov, Sergey Samsonov

item.title: Mode Collapse of Mean-Field Variational Inference
item.description: arXiv:2510.17063v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mean-field variational inference (MFVI) is a widely used method for approximating high-dimensional probability distributions by product measures. It has been empirically observed that MFVI optimizers often suffer from \emph{mode collapse}. For example, when the target measure $\pi$ is a mixture $\pi = w P_0 + (1 - w) P_1$, the MFVI optimizer tends to place most of its mass near a single component of the mixture. This work provides the first \emph{theoretical} explanation of mode collapse in MFVI. Starting from two-component mixtures, we introduce the notion of \emph{$\varepsilon$-separateness} to quantify the separation of the mixture components. We derive explicit bounds on the mass that any MFVI optimizer assigns to each component, when $P_0$ and $P_1$ are $\varepsilon$-separated for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. We further extend this analysis to mixture target distributions with multiple components. Our results reveal that the occurrence of mode collapse crucially depends on the relative position of the components. To address this issue, we propose \emph{rotational variational inference (RoVI)}, which augments MFVI with a rotation matrix. The numerical studies support our theoretical findings and illustrate improved mode coverage with RoVI in Bayesian mixture posteriors, including a real-data example.
item.dc:creator: Shunan Sheng, Bohan Wu, Alberto Gonz\'alez-Sanz

item.title: Complexity Dependent Error Rates for Physics-informed Statistical Learning via the Small-ball Method
item.description: arXiv:2510.23149v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Physics-informed statistical learning (PISL) integrates empirical data with physical knowledge to enhance the statistical performance of estimators. While PISL methods are widely used in practice, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of how informed regularization affects statistical properties is still missing. Specifically, two fundamental questions have yet to be fully addressed: (A) what is the trade-off between soft penalties and hard constraints, and (B) what is the statistical gain of incorporating physical knowledge compared to purely data-driven empirical error minimisation. In this paper, we address these questions for PISL in classes of functions whose convex hull satisfies a small-ball condition, in particular convex classes, under physical knowledge expressed as linear equations by developing appropriate complexity dependent error rates based on the small-ball method. We specialise them to linear classes of finite dimension $q$ in which the space of solutions of the equation has dimension $k < q$, and show that (A) the physics-informed estimator attains the error bound of the hard-constrained empirical error minimiser whenever the penalty parameter is above an explicit threshold, and that (B) the penalty improves the error rate from $\sqrt{q/n}$ to $\sqrt{k/n}$ under a second moment condition on the noise only, having the effect of a dimensionality reduction. We also quantify how these conclusions degrade when the equation is misspecified, in terms of the excess residual of the target function. This work establishes a theoretical framework for evaluating the statistical properties of physics-informed estimators in such classes, contributing to closing the gap between statistical theory and practical PISL.
item.dc:creator: Diego Marcondes

item.title: Self-sufficient Independent Component Analysis for Demixing Flows
item.description: arXiv:2512.00665v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the problem of learning disentangled signals from data using non-linear Independent Component Analysis (ICA). Motivated by advances in self-supervised learning, we propose to learn self-sufficient signals: Given the remaining values of a recovered signal, observing other signals should not change the conditional distribution of its missing value. We formulate this problem as the minimization of a conditional KL divergence. Our algorithm is prior-free and likelihood-free in the sense that it prescribes neither parametric source densities nor an observation likelihood. To tackle the KL divergence minimization problem, we propose a sequential algorithm that learns a de-mixing flow model at each iteration, and prove local descent of the total correlation for its idealized Wasserstein-gradient-flow variant with exact velocities and a population projection condition. This approach completely avoids the unstable adversarial training, a common issue in minimizing the KL divergence. Experiments on toy and real-world datasets show the effectiveness of our method.
item.dc:creator: Song Liu

item.title: Control Consistency Losses for Diffusion Bridges
item.description: arXiv:2512.05070v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulating the conditioned dynamics of diffusion processes, given their initial and terminal states, is an important but challenging problem in the sciences. The difficulty is particularly pronounced for rare events, for which the unconditioned dynamics rarely reach the terminal state. In this work, we propose a novel approach for learning diffusion bridges based on a self-consistency property of the optimal control. The resulting algorithm learns the conditioned dynamics in an iterative online manner, and exhibits strong performance in a range of empirical settings without requiring differentiation through simulated trajectories. Beyond the diffusion bridge setting, we draw connections between our self-consistency framework and recent advances in the wider stochastic optimal control literature.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Howard, Nikolas N\"usken, Jakiw Pidstrigach

item.title: Sampling from multimodal distributions with warm starts: Non-asymptotic bounds for the Reweighted Annealed Leap-Point Sampler
item.description: arXiv:2512.17977v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sampling from multimodal distributions is a central challenge in Bayesian inference and machine learning. In light of hardness results for sampling -- classical MCMC methods, even with tempering, can suffer from exponential mixing times -- a natural question is how to leverage additional information, such as a warm start point for each mode, to enable faster mixing across modes. To address this, we introduce Reweighted ALPS (Re-ALPS), a modified version of the Annealed Leap-Point Sampler (ALPS) that dispenses with the Gaussian approximation assumption. We prove the first polynomial-time bound that works in a general setting, under a natural assumption that each component contains significant mass relative to the others when tilted towards the corresponding warm start point. Similarly to ALPS, we define distributions tilted towards a mixture centered at the warm start points, and at the coldest level, use teleportation between warm start points to enable efficient mixing across modes. In contrast to ALPS, our method does not require Hessian information at the modes, but instead estimates component partition functions via Monte Carlo. This additional estimation step is crucial in allowing the algorithm to handle target distributions with more complex geometries besides approximate Gaussian. For the proof, we show convergence results for Markov processes when only part of the stationary distribution is well-mixing and estimation for partition functions for individual components of a mixture.
item.dc:creator: Holden Lee, Matheau Santana-Gijzen

item.title: Nonparametric Kernel Clustering with Bandit Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2601.07535v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Clustering with bandit feedback refers to the problem of partitioning the arms of an $N$-armed stochastic bandit according to their underlying distributions, based on noisy observations collected sequentially and adaptively. This setting has attracted growing interest for its applicability in recommendation systems, crowdsourcing, and adaptive trials. Existing works rely on the strong assumption that arm distributions are sub-Gaussian, which can only distinguish arms whose distributions differ in mean - missing realistic settings where distributional differences lie in shape or higher moments. % We introduce a framework of \emph{nonparametric clustering with bandit feedback}, free of any parametric assumptions regarding the arm distributions. We adopt a kernel-based approach and reformulate the problem as clustering arms according to their kernel mean embeddings in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Building on this formulation, we introduce the \kabc\ algorithm, prove that it is $\delta$-PAC, and derive a non-asymptotic high-probability upper bound on its sampling complexity. The bound is governed by a variance-aware signal-to-noise ratio defined as the minimum over pairs of arms in distinct clusters of the ratio between their squared MMD and their RKHS variance. \kabc\ achieves instance-dependent guarantees while being adaptive to this unknown ratio. We validate our approach empirically on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating that \kabc\ succeeds in distributional clustering settings where mean-based methods fail.
item.dc:creator: Victor Thuot (MISTEA, UMPA-ENSL), Sebastian Vogt (LRR-TUM), Debarghya Ghoshdastidar (LRR-TUM), Nicolas Verzelen (MISTEA)

item.title: When Does Trimming Help Conformal Prediction? A Retained-Law Diagnostic under Calibration Contamination
item.description: arXiv:2605.06204v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Trimming suspicious calibration points is a common response to contamination in conformal prediction. Its effect on clean-target coverage, however, is governed by the retained law induced by trimming, not by the contamination level alone. We analyse fixed-threshold trimming as conditioning rather than purification. It replaces the contaminated calibration law with a retained law, reducing clean-target coverage to a one-dimensional score-CDF transfer problem with an exact finite-sample identity. A componentwise bound on the transfer gap gives a population-level diagnostic. This separates a clean-side covariance cost from a retained-contamination cost, governed by the dirty-to-clean retention ratio. Trimming helps when the anomaly score separates retention probabilities while remaining score-neutral on the clean population. Otherwise, it cannot substantially reduce contamination through the retained mixture coefficient. We also give finite-sample certificate templates that provide numerical guarantees under independent audit.
item.dc:creator: Congye Wang

item.title: Federated Language Models Under Bandwidth Budgets: Distillation Rates and Conformal Coverage
item.description: arXiv:2605.09986v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hospitals, companies, and research consortia want language models that learn from, and answer questions over, data that must stay where it is held, over links with limited bandwidth, such as the satellite links of remote clinics and ships. Averaging the sites' model parameters makes each message grow with the model and requires one shared architecture; methods that exchange predictions avoid both limits, but, to our knowledge, none bounds what compressing those predictions costs. We introduce two methods that compress every message at a small and predictable cost. Federated Probe-Logit Distillation (FPLD) trains a shared language model: each site sends compressed logits on shared unlabeled probes, and a hub distills one model from their average. Federated Conformal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (FC-RAG) answers questions: each site scores candidate answers using its own documents and sends compressed scores, and the hub returns a conformal prediction set that contains the correct answer at a guaranteed rate. Both use one codec, which centers each message and rounds it after adding a random offset known to the receiver. For logits within a fixed clipping range, we bound the expected log-loss added by compression independently of vocabulary size; the bound depends only on the bits, the range, and the number of sites, falls as more sites take part, and lets the bit budget be set before deployment. We also prove that recalibrating after compression keeps the coverage guarantee, and that FPLD's training error bounds how far coverage can slip when a threshold is reused after a model update. In experiments with GPT-2 and Qwen2.5, 8 bits per number cause no detectable loss in the trained model or in coverage. FPLD also trains a shared model across different architectures, where parameter averaging does not apply; with one shared architecture, parameter averaging remains more accurate.
item.dc:creator: Prasanjit Dubey, Xiaoming Huo

item.title: $\alpha$-TCAV: A Unified Framework for Testing with Concept Activation Vectors
item.description: arXiv:2605.15688v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Concept Activation Vectors (CAV) and the Testing with CAVs (TCAV) method are fundamental tools for concept-based explainability in deep learning, yet their practical utility is limited by the variability across different samples of concept and non-concept examples. We analyze this stochastic nature of CAVs, and identify a fundamental flaw in the standard TCAV score, its instability by using a discontinuous indicator function. To address this, we introduce $\alpha$-TCAV, a parameterized unified framework that replaces the discontinuous indicator with a smooth function, which recovers TCAV as a limiting case. Under realistic assumptions, we characterize the score distributions and derive principled parameter choices: one matches the mean of its averaged counterpart, Multi-TCAV, with no larger variance using a single CAV; the other provides a calibrated probability that the concept positively influences the model output. Our analysis and experiments provide practical guidance and challenge the established practice of splitting the sampling budget across multiple CAVs.
item.dc:creator: Ekkehard Schnoor, Jawher Said, Malik Tiomoko, Wojciech Samek, Alexander Jung

item.title: On Finite-sample Concentration of Median of Incomplete U-Statistics
item.description: arXiv:2606.00661v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Median-of-means (MoM) is a powerful technique that theoretically enables near sub-Gaussian finite-sample rate for parameter estimation when the underlying data distribution is heavy-tailed (e.g., assumed to have only two first finite moments). A recent work has extrapolated this technique to median-of-\textit{randomized}-U-Statistics (MoRU) and median-of-\textit{incomplete}-U-Statistics (MoIU) for estimating expectations of heavy-tailed pairwise kernels. In \citet{pmlr-v97-clemencon19a}, a concentration rate that scales like $O(n^{-1/2})$ with sample size has been proven for MoRU. However, despite the computational advantage of the latter, the analysis of finite-sample bound for MoIU remains a significant theoretical challenge. As noted by the authors, a straightforward application of McDiarmid's inequality yields a loose bound of order $O(n^{-1/4})$. In this work, we prove a finite-sample concentration bound for the MoIU estimator that scales as $O(n^{-1/2})$ with respect to the sample size using a delicate convex decomposition approach. Furthermore, we show that our proof can be seamlessly extended to geometric median in multivariate settings. Using a Serfling-type argument, we extrapolate our results into a regime where data pairs are selected without replacement across blocks, breaking the usual block-wise independence condition. Then, using a Bernstein-type treatment for U-Statistics, we tighten the dependency of our bounds on the margin $\tau$ from $O(\tau^{-3/2})$ achieved in the previous work to $O(\tau^{-1})$. Finally, we proved anti-concentration results that is applicable for all median estimators presented in this work to demonstrate that $M\le O(n)$ is an intrinsic restriction on block sizes.
item.dc:creator: Nong Minh Hieu, Antoine Ledent

item.title: Beyond Cultural Persona Bias: Response Geometry as a Measure for Language Models and People
item.description: arXiv:2607.02368v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Researchers are increasingly prompting language models with cultural personas so that they answer questionnaires as diverse human groups would. However, studies often report that these persona responses do not predict the models' behavior. We argue that whether the persona is Western or non-Western, the model's answers carry a cultural preference, and that this preference masks the variables that could predict its behavior. We examine the prompted preference at two levels: aggregate Big Five scores and response geometry, the correlation matrix between dimensions within each respondent, represented as a symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrix. In DeepSeek-V3 and GPT-4o, when the item order is fixed, the prompted preference appears at both levels. Randomizing item order reduces it in the response geometry, while leaving it in the Big Five scores: the Big Five still separate the two personas at $95$--$97\%$, while response geometry falls to chance. In randomized administration, the response geometry still contains information about the respondent. In DeepSeek-V4-Flash, SPD features are associated with whether the same instance sorts Asian American public figures as ``foreign'' in a text IAT ($p = .047$), while the Big Five do not. In human studies conducted using randomized item order, the response geometry identifies people from test-retest sessions in $81$ -- $85\%$, against chance $0.4\%$, and predicts sex and, weakly, age. In addition, SPD features also predict complex human behavior (e.g., cumulative GPA, $R^2 = 0.28$, permutation $p = .003$), where the Big Five do not.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Yuan

item.title: Why Learning Rediscovers the Closed-Form Diagonal Regularizer
item.description: arXiv:2609.09656v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recovering modal amplitudes from a few sensors requires regularization, and the shape of the penalty decides how strongly each mode is shrunk. The best shape depends on the truncation noise that discarded modes add to every measurement, which is unobserved and could be room-specific. We identify a diagonal saturation principle: for a single snapshot, isotropic truncation noise makes the Bayes-optimal Tikhonov shape a closed-form power law Gamma_k proportional to lambda_k^|s|, set by the prior alone and independent of the domain. The off-diagonal anisotropy equals the Herfindahl index H of the discarded-mode power exactly, Weyl's eigenvalue counting law fixes the number of discarded modes and hence H, and Berry's random-wave conjecture enters only through a diagonal term D, which we measure directly. Together they predict an approximately flat loss landscape over the penalty exponent, which leaves a learned diagonal regularizer little to gain from tuning the exponent per room. On simulated acoustic rooms the closed form stays within 5.83% of a per-room power-law oracle across observation windows, and three learned diagonal architectures track its error, the closest within a fraction of a point and none more than 3pp above it, while learning qualitatively different spectra. In the truncation regime no tested method consistently improves on the closed form, including Learned Iterative Ridge, which couples modes across layers. The framework extends to heat diffusion through a known Green's-function correction with no new free parameters.
item.dc:creator: Jeahn Han, Pyojin Kim

item.title: OSCAR: Order-aware Sensitivity Correction for AI Rankings
item.description: arXiv:2609.24128v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM judges evaluate candidate language models through pairwise comparisons of their responses. Judge-aware Bradley--Terry models aggregate pairwise comparisons by jointly estimating candidate scores and judge-specific sensitivities (how strongly each judge responds to quality differences), often interpreted as reliability. We show that this reading fails when judges prefer a display position. Even under balanced display orders or swap-and-average, omitting position attenuates fitted judge sensitivity by approximately the factor $1-D^2$ near equal quality, where $D$ is the judge's net first-slot preference between equally good responses. We propose OSCAR, which jointly estimates candidate scores, judge sensitivities and judge-specific position, length and family effects, and provides confidence intervals for pairwise win probabilities that account for dependence within prompts. On held-out data, observed attenuation closely matches the prediction $1-D^2$ (correlation of log ratios 0.99). Across four datasets, position adjustment lowers held-out log loss by 14-23% and changes which judges would be dropped for low sensitivity on three datasets. On MT-Bench, it ranks GPT-4 first instead of claude-v1, matching human votes. Simulations with known parameters show improved recovery of judge sensitivities and candidate rankings, with 94.4-95.2% confidence interval coverage. Low estimated sensitivity alone is therefore not evidence of an unreliable judge.
item.dc:creator: You Liu, Yue Liu, Quanchao Lu, Ergan Shang, Nick Shipilov

item.title: PICPIs: Prediction-Interval-Conditional Prediction Intervals
item.description: arXiv:2609.25388v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A classical question in statistics is which observable quantities to condition on when drawing inferences about unobservable targets. For conformal prediction in nonparametric uncertainty quantification, standard marginal validity offers limited resolution at the prediction values on which decisions are based, and fully conditional guarantees with respect to the covariates are provably unattainable. We address this gap by introducing a prediction-based conditioning framework that we refer to as Prediction-Interval-Conditional Prediction Intervals (PICPIs). Formally, a PICPI is an interval $I$ satisfying a self-consistency condition: $$\mathbb{E} [Y \mid p(X) \in I] \in I,$$ for predictive model $p$, contextual covariate $X$, and outcome $Y$. Thus, an interval simultaneously defines a stratum of prediction values and certifies that the mean outcome in that stratum lies in the same interval. This self-consistency condition yields data-adaptive strata without altering the original prediction. Such intervals can be constructed using practical algorithms. Under regularity of the prediction distribution, the constructed intervals cover all but an arbitrarily small fraction of prediction values and have widths that decrease at rate $n^{-1/3}$, up to logarithmic factors and the prediction error. Moreover, identifying these locally calibrated intervals can, in turn, inform downstream decision-making. We derive inference procedures for PICPIs in probabilistic prediction and multi-class classification, accompanied by theoretical guarantees. Empirical results are provided that compare PICPIs with existing interval-based baselines.
item.dc:creator: Xuelin Yang, Baihe Huang, Yilong Hou, Guido Imbens, Michael I. Jordan

item.title: Multi-Marginal Inverse Optimal Transport for Contrastive Learning Via Explicit Anchor-Positive-Negative Coupling
item.description: arXiv:2609.33741v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inverse Optimal Transport (OT) based methods for representation learning learn representations such that the global OT coupling between a pair of data marginals in the representation space, concentrates on the positive pairs. This is in contrast to previous methods that primarily focused on pairwise matching. However, these methods $\textit{DO NOT}$ utilize negative pairs and hence are not truly contrastive in their approach. We show that this leads to issues of dimensional collapse and hence degraded downstream performance. To alleviate this, we develop a novel multi-marginal (MM) inverse OT (IOT) contrastive learning (CL) approach called Neg-MMIOT-CL, which learns representations such that the global multi-marginal OT (MMOT) coupling between a triple of data marginals, with respect to a carefully designed ground-cost between triplets of data points in the representation space, concentrates on the anchor-positive-negative $\textit{triplets}$. For a latent class model, we empirically show that Neg-MMIOT-CL alleviates dimensional collapse. Furthermore, for a specific choice of ground cost for all triplets in representation space, we prove that the optimal representation configuration for Neg-MMIOT-CL exhibits equiangular property for within-class and across-class representations, which translates to Neural-Collapse when the representation dimension is larger than the number of classes minus one -- a result that is $\textit{previously established only}$ for pairwise contrastive learning methods. Finally, we propose Neg-IOT-CL-PushPull, that is a computationally efficient alternative to Neg-MMIOT-CL, alleviating the high cost of computing MMOT plans needed during implementation. We apply these methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets and show significant improvements over existing OT-based contrastive learning methods.
item.dc:creator: Ngoc-Hai Nguyen, Thuan Nguyen, Prakash Ishwar, Shuchin Aeron

item.title: Amortized Structured Stochastic Variational Inference for Gaussian Process Latent Variable Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.03647v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many machine learning methods aim to approximate the lower-dimensional manifold on which the data lives. A desirable feature of such methods is that they should capture the epistemic uncertainty of this learned manifold. One model that achieves this is the Gaussian Process Latent Variable Model, in which a Gaussian Process (GP) mapping from the latent space provides an estimate of the uncertainty of the manifold. However, the effectiveness of this uncertainty estimation is limited by the mean-field variational approximation between the GP inducing points and the latent variables. In this work, we apply Amortized Structured Stochastic Variational Inference to allow the variational posterior for the latent space to be conditionally dependent on the value of the inducing points. We demonstrate that this more flexible variational posterior improves several metrics relating to the reconstruction of points on the data manifold.
item.dc:creator: Maksym Tretiakov, Sarah Filippi, Vincent Fortuin, Ruth Misener, Ruby Sedgwick, James Odgers

item.title: Targeted Active Learning for Preference-Based Treatment Effects on Multivariate Outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2610.03824v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Treatment efficacy is traditionally demonstrated on the basis of a single primary outcome. However, clinical decision-making usually requires consideration of multiple outcomes, balancing expected benefits against potential risks. The relative value assigned to these outcomes varies substantially from one patient to another. Given a preference rule over outcome profiles, treatment effects and optimal policies can be defined and estimated. Such a rule is rarely available in practice: it must itself be estimated from pairwise comparisons of outcome profiles, which are costly to collect from clinical experts. We propose an active learning framework that selects which comparisons to query. Standard criteria maximize the information gained on the preference rule itself. We instead target the quantities of interest, and select the query that most reduces uncertainty on the treatment effect and on the optimal policy induced by the learned rule. Under a Gaussian process model of the preference rule, we derive a closed-form approximation of this criterion. On semi-synthetic data built from a Parkinson's disease cohort with 13 clinical outcomes, our criterion achieves lower treatment effect estimation error and lower policy regret than existing criteria at equal query budget.
item.dc:creator: Lola Giordani, Mathieu Even, Chlo\'e Geoffroy, Jean-Christophe Corvol, Rapha\"el Porcher, Federico Pavone

item.title: Retrieval-Based In-Context Learning: A Domain Adaptation Framework
item.description: arXiv:2610.05717v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In-context retrieval (ICR) is a retrieval-based form of in-context learning (ICL) in which demonstrations are retrieved from a source database based on similarity to the query, rather than sampled independently. In this work, we formulate ICR as a type of domain adaptation problem, where the source distribution $P$ of the database may differ from the target distribution $Q$ of the test query-label pair. We investigate the performance of ICR under a flexible class of distributional shifts that substantially extends prior work \citep{li2024fine,guo2025retrieval}, and establish theoretical guarantees that quantify the benefits and pitfalls of this learning paradigm. Our theory is verified by experiments on synthetic and language tasks.
item.dc:creator: Yilun Zhu, Naihao Deng, Yingcong Li, Naichen Shi, Clayton Scott

item.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent Ascent is Suboptimal for Nonconvex-P{\L} Min-Max Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.07814v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How far can stochastic gradient descent ascent (SGDA) go by tuning its timescale ratio and step sizes in nonconvex min-max games? We answer this question for nonconvex-P{\L} (NC-P{\L}) games by establishing the first tight complexity of two-timescale SGDA with a fixed timescale ratio and non-increasing step sizes. For $\ell$-smooth games with an inner $\mu$-P{\L} inequality, we prove a complexity lower bound $\Omega(\kappa^2\ell\varepsilon^{-2}+\kappa^4\ell\sigma^2\varepsilon^{-4})$, where $\kappa=\ell/\mu$ is the condition number, $\sigma^2$ is the gradient variance, and $\varepsilon$ measures the outer gradient norm. This matches existing SGDA upper bounds and establishes a complexity separation from Smoothed-AGDA (Yang et al., 22'). In addition, we show that SGDA can fail to find a stationary point when its timescale ratio is as small as $o(\kappa^2)$. Our negative results highlight the fundamental limitation of SGDA in NC-P{\L} games, and justify the development of alternative methods.
item.dc:creator: Junsoo Ha

item.title: Differentiable Systematic Resampling for Variational Sequential Monte Carlo
item.description: arXiv:2610.12094v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Particle filters are a standard tool for nonlinear state estimation, but their resampling step is discrete, preventing gradient-based learning in variational sequential Monte Carlo. We introduce Differentiable Systematic Resampling (DSR), a temperature-controlled relaxation of systematic resampling, that preserves the CDF-ordered, banded structure of systematic resampling while enabling full gradient flow. DSR converges to exact systematic resampling as the temperature vanishes, and we prove a pointwise exponential convergence rate for the induced bias. Compared to optimal-transport-based differentiable resampling, DSR avoids iterative solvers and has substantially lower computational overhead. Experiments on stochastic dynamical systems and real-world handwriting data show that DSR achieves comparable or superior filtering and dynamics learning performance.
item.dc:creator: Fredrik Cumlin, Saikat Chatterjee

item.title: ISBO: Scalable Spatio-Temporal Bayesian Optimization with Log Gaussian Cox Process Models via the INLA-SPDE Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.12213v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) is a popular method for efficiently optimizing expensive black-box objectives. However, BO utilizing standard Gaussian Processes is ill-suited for doubly stochastic Cox Processes that are often used in spatio-temporal problem spaces. We introduce INLA-SPDE Spatio-Temporal Bayesian Optimization (ISBO): the first scalable BO framework for spatio-temporal data, that models the log-intensity with a Log-Gaussian Cox Process(LGCP) and performs inference via Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation and Stochastic Partial Differential Equations (INLA-SPDE) approach. Using a Matern field on meshes yields a sparse Gaussian Markov Random Field, where INLA provides fast and accurate posterior inference throughout sequential optimization. ISBO stably locates high-intensity regions and the peak of the latent intensity with minimal evaluations. A time-varying Upper Confidence Bound acquisition with masking avoids revisits, while penalized-complexity priors regularize early rounds. Experiments on synthetic and real-world spatio-temporal datasets show accurate peak discovery, intensity recovery, and substantial speedups over an RKHS-based baseline, positioning ISBO as a practical choice for BO with point-process data.
item.dc:creator: Kaichuang Yang, H{\aa}vard Rue, Jakob Zeitler

item.title: Density Ratio Estimation with Stein Displacement Fields
item.description: arXiv:2610.12437v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Density ratios quantify distribution shift from a probability-mass point of view, whereas displacement fields describe, from a dynamical point of view, how one distribution is transported onto another. Although both offer complementary insights, they are usually estimated separately, and converting one into the other requires post-processing. In this paper, we estimate the density ratio between a target and a base distribution by parametrizing it through a displacement field acting on the base: the log-ratio is modeled as minus the Stein operator of the base applied to the field, up to a normalizing constant. This gives both statistical and dynamical descriptions of the distribution shift through a single convex optimization problem. Iterating this estimate-and-move step gives two inference algorithms: push-forward moves the model and corrects a pretrained sampler without retraining it, whereas pull-back moves the data closer to the base and fits a transformation model one layer at a time. Applications to distribution shift in simulation-based inference and to nonlinear independent component analysis illustrate the benefits and limitations of the approach.
item.dc:creator: Song Liu

item.title: Semantic Context Forests for Learning-Based Knee Cartilage Segmentation in 3D MR Images
item.description: arXiv:1307.2965v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The automatic segmentation of human knee cartilage from 3D MR images is a useful yet challenging task due to the thin sheet structure of the cartilage with diffuse boundaries and inhomogeneous intensities. In this paper, we present an iterative multi-class learning method to segment the femoral, tibial and patellar cartilage simultaneously, which effectively exploits the spatial contextual constraints between bone and cartilage, and also between different cartilages. First, based on the fact that the cartilage grows in only certain area of the corresponding bone surface, we extract the distance features of not only to the surface of the bone, but more informatively, to the densely registered anatomical landmarks on the bone surface. Second, we introduce a set of iterative discriminative classifiers that at each iteration, probability comparison features are constructed from the class confidence maps derived by previously learned classifiers. These features automatically embed the semantic context information between different cartilages of interest. Validated on a total of 176 volumes from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) dataset, the proposed approach demonstrates high robustness and accuracy of segmentation in comparison with existing state-of-the-art MR cartilage segmentation methods. Code: https://github.com/wq2012/kneeseg Pretrained Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/wq2012/knee-mri-segmentation
item.dc:creator: Quan Wang, Dijia Wu, Le Lu, Meizhu Liu, Kim L. Boyer, Shaohua Kevin Zhou

item.title: Concentration inequalities for leave-one-out cross validation
item.description: arXiv:2211.02478v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this article we prove that estimator stability, together with a gradient-growth condition on the expected fitted loss, is enough to provide concentration bounds for leave-one-out cross-validation in a general framework. In particular, we provide concentration bounds beyond Lipschitz continuity assumptions on the loss or on the estimator. We obtain our results by relying on random variables with distribution satisfying the logarithmic Sobolev inequality, providing us a relatively rich class of distributions. We illustrate our method by considering several interesting examples, including linear regression, kernel density estimation, and stabilized/truncated estimators such as stabilized kernel regression.
item.dc:creator: Benny Avelin, Lauri Viitasaari

item.title: Optimal Transport Aggregation for Distributed Mixture-of-Experts
item.description: arXiv:2312.09877v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper considers the setting in which local Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models are fitted independently on distributed datasets and must be combined into a single global MoE model. Weighted averaging the local mixtures, whose experts are not aligned across machines, often yields a large mixture with many experts instead of $K$ and does not provide an estimator of the true model parameters. We propose to reduce this large mixture to a $K$-expert MoE by minimizing an expected transportation divergence, in which the transport plan depends on the covariates. A relaxation of this problem separates the experts from the gating network: the experts are computed by a majorization--minimization algorithm, which decreases the objective monotonically, and the gating network is then fitted to the gates implied by the optimal plan, with an explicit bound on the resulting loss. We show that the aggregated estimator is consistent whenever the local estimators are, without requiring the local models to have the same labeling across machines. The procedure only needs a single one-way communication round. Experiments on simulated and real data show accuracy close to centralized estimation at a fraction of its computation time. Our source code is available at https://github.com/nhat-thien/Distributed-Mixture-Of-Experts.
item.dc:creator: Fa\"icel Chamroukhi, Nhat Thien Pham

item.title: Targeted Data Fusion for Region-Specific Survival Effects in the AMP HIV Prevention Trials
item.description: arXiv:2501.18798v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Antibody Mediated Prevention (AMP) trials opened a new scientific frontier by showing that passively administered monoclonal broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) could prevent HIV-1 acquisition. The trials enrolled 4,611 participants across four epidemiologically distinct regions, with 174 HIV-1 diagnoses observed during follow-up. Regional heterogeneity in treatment efficacy, together with privacy and regulatory limits on central data pooling, calls for methods that borrow strength across regions without sharing individual-level data. To estimate region- and treatment-specific survival curves under distributional heterogeneity, we develop a federated learning approach that combines site-specific estimators via an L1-regularized criterion that downweights data sources not aligned with the target. We further extend the framework to a general class of causal contrasts, including the survival difference, survival ratio, and restricted mean survival time difference. In the AMP analysis, for example, the standard error of the day-148 survival difference decreased from 0.007 using the target-only estimator to 0.004 using the federated estimator. For women in South Africa, the region-specific analyses provided no strong evidence of an overall VRC01 benefit, consistent with the primary AMP findings. Overall, the proposed approach provides region-adaptive inference with improved precision without sharing individual-level data, while preserving estimation of region-specific treatment effects under cross-region heterogeneity.
item.dc:creator: Yi Liu, Alexander W. Levis, Ke Zhu, Shu Yang, Peter B. Gilbert, Larry Han

item.title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data via APIs 3: Using Simulators Instead of Foundation Model
item.description: arXiv:2502.05505v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Differentially private (DP) synthetic data enables the use of sensitive datasets while providing strong privacy guarantees. Recently, Private Evolution (PE) has emerged as a promising framework for generating DP synthetic data using only inference APIs of foundation models. However, suitable foundation models are not always available for every private data domain. In this paper, we show that PE is more general than previously understood and can incorporate APIs beyond foundation models. In particular, we show that state-of-the-art non-neural-network data synthesizers, including computer graphics-based image generators and physics simulation tools (which we refer to as simulators), integrate naturally into PE. We call the resulting method Sim-PE. Sim-PE broadens the applicability of PE while improving performance. For image synthesis, Sim-PE improves downstream classification accuracy by up to 3x, reduces FID by up to 80%, and is significantly more efficient. We further show that simulators and foundation models can be seamlessly combined within Sim-PE for additional gains. Beyond performance improvements, Sim-PE enables new DP applications that are difficult or impossible for existing methods, including generating DP control signals whose execution reproduces the distribution of private observations. The code is open-sourced in the Private Evolution Python library: https://github.com/microsoft/DPSDA
item.dc:creator: Zinan Lin, Tadas Baltrusaitis, Wenyu Wang, Sergey Yekhanin

item.title: Stein's unbiased risk estimate and Hyv\"arinen's score matching
item.description: arXiv:2502.20123v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Given a collection of observed signals corrupted with Gaussian noise, how can we learn to optimally denoise them? This fundamental problem arises in both empirical Bayes and generative modeling. In empirical Bayes, the predominant approach is via nonparametric maximum likelihood estimation (NPMLE), while in generative modeling, score matching (SM) methods have proven very successful. In our setting, Hyv\"arinen's implicit SM is equivalent to another classical idea from statistics---Stein's Unbiased Risk Estimate (SURE). Revisiting SURE minimization, we establish, for the first time, that SURE achieves nearly parametric rates of convergence of the regret in the classical empirical Bayes setting with homoscedastic noise. We also prove that SURE-training can achieve fast rates of convergence to the oracle denoiser in a commonly studied misspecified model. We show how to practically implement our method in settings involving heteroscedasticity and side-information, such as in an application to the estimation of economic mobility in the Opportunity Atlas. Our empirical results demonstrate the superior performance of SURE-training over NPMLE under misspecification. Collectively, our findings advance SURE/SM as a strong alternative to the NPMLE for empirical Bayes problems in both theory and practice.
item.dc:creator: Sulagna Ghosh, Nikolaos Ignatiadis, Frederic Koehler, Amber Lee

item.title: The Serial Scaling Hypothesis
item.description: arXiv:2507.12549v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While machine learning has advanced through massive parallelization, we identify a critical blind spot: some problems are fundamentally sequential. These "inherently serial" problems-from mathematical reasoning to physical simulations to sequential decision-making-require sequentially dependent computational steps that cannot be efficiently parallelized. We formalize this distinction in complexity theory, and demonstrate that current parallel-centric architectures face fundamental limitations on such tasks. Then, we show for first time that diffusion models despite their sequential nature are incapable of solving inherently serial problems. We argue that recognizing the serial nature of computation holds profound implications on machine learning, model design, and hardware development.
item.dc:creator: Yuxi Liu, Konpat Preechakul, Kananart Kuwaranancharoen, Yutong Bai

item.title: Bouncy particle sampler with infinite exchanging parallel tempering
item.description: arXiv:2509.02003v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Markov chain Monte Carlo is one of the most useful tools for obtaining samples from complex distributions, such as posterior distributions in Bayesian inference. Bouncy particle sampler (BPS) is a method that performs sampling using uniform linear motion and elastic collisions. Since BPS does not require time discretization, it is expected to be more advantageous than the widely used Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) and Langevin Monte Carlo (LMC) for distributions with large curvature changes. To sample more efficiently from multimodal distributions, we propose BPS with parallel tempering (BPS-PT) in the infinite exchange limit, based on LMC-PT with the infinite exchange rate proposed in a previous study. Using a distribution with large curvature changes, BPS-PT showed estimation accuracy comparable to HMC-PT and LMC-PT, and achieved higher ESS per computational time. Therefore, BPS-PT is considered to be effective for distributions with large curvature changes.
item.dc:creator: Yohei Saito, Shun Kimura, Koujin Takeda

item.title: Metadata-Guided Adaptable Frequency Scaling across Heterogeneous Applications and Devices
item.description: arXiv:2509.22707v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling is essential for enhancing energy efficiency in mobile platforms. However, traditional heuristic-based governors are increasingly inadequate for managing the complexity of heterogeneous System-on-Chip designs and diverse application workloads. Although reinforcement learning approaches offer improved performance, their poor generalization capability and reliance on extensive retraining for each hardware and application combination leads to significant deployment costs. In this work, we observe that device and application metadata inherently encapsulate valuable knowledge for DVFS, presenting an opportunity to overcome these limitations. We formulate DVFS for heterogeneous devices and applications as a multi-task reinforcement learning problem. We introduce MetaDVFS, which is a metadata-guided framework that systematically leverages metadata to discover and transfer shared knowledge across DVFS tasks. MetaDVFS can output a set of DVFS models with significant generalization capability for various applications of heterogeneous devices. Evaluations on five Google Pixel devices running six applications show that MetaDVFS achieves up to 17% improvement in Performance-Power Ratio and up to 26% improvement in Quality of Experience. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, MetaDVFS delivers 70.8% faster adaptation and 5.8-27.6% higher performance over standalone device-application specific training, while avoiding negative transfer effects. These results establish MetaDVFS as an effective and scalable solution for DVFS deployment in heterogeneous mobile environments.
item.dc:creator: Jinqi Yan, Fang He, Qianlong Sang, Bifeng Tong, Peng Sun, Yili Gong, Chuang Hu, Dazhao Cheng

item.title: Rethinking Langevin Thompson Sampling from A Stochastic Approximation Perspective
item.description: arXiv:2510.05023v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Langevin-based Thompson Sampling (TS) methods for multi-armed bandits use likelihood gradients to approximate posterior samples when exact sampling is intractable. As new rewards arrive, the posterior changes, and these methods run an inner Markov chain to approximate the updated target. To simplify this repeated sampling procedure, we introduce TS-SA, which incorporates stochastic approximation (SA) within the TS framework. In each round, TS-SA takes one Langevin step using the newly observed reward and applies an SA update to combine the noisy proposal with the current parameter estimate. By retaining this estimate across rounds, TS-SA maintains one continuing Markov chain for each arm, preserving the influence of past observations without storing or sampling them again. Within this recursion, the proposal step size remains fixed across rounds, while the SA weights decrease as observations accumulate to control the effect of noise on the estimate. This continuing-chain formulation simplifies the theoretical analysis, allowing us to establish a near-optimal worst-case regret bound of $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\sqrt{KT})$ under log-concavity and smoothness assumptions with one update per new reward. Our experiments further demonstrate that TS-SA, using a single-step Langevin update after an initial warm-up, achieves strong performance against standard baselines.
item.dc:creator: Weixin Wang, Haoyang Zheng, Guang Lin, Wei Deng, Pan Xu

item.title: Bayesian Optimization under Uncertainty for Training a Scale Parameter in Stochastic Models
item.description: arXiv:2510.06439v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hyperparameter tuning is a challenging problem especially when the system itself involves uncertainty. Due to noisy function evaluations, optimization under uncertainty can be computationally expensive. In this paper, we present a novel Bayesian optimization framework tailored for hyperparameter tuning under uncertainty, with a focus on optimizing a scale- or precision-type parameter in stochastic models. The proposed method employs a statistical surrogate for the underlying random variable, enabling analytical evaluation of the expectation operator. Moreover, we derive a closed-form expression for the optimizer of the random acquisition function, which significantly reduces computational cost per iteration. Numerical experiments demonstrate substantial gains in optimization efficiency: about 40-fold reduction in data usage relative to a Monte Carlo-based one-dimensional optimization scheme, and an order of magnitude improvement relative to a Gaussian process-based Bayesian optimization baseline.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: ASCE-ASME J. Risk Uncertainty Eng. Syst., Part A: Civ. Eng. 12(4): 04026050 (2026)
item.dc:creator: Akash Yadav, Ruda Zhang

item.title: Batch Bayesian Active Learning with Partial Batch Label Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2510.09877v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Over the past couple of decades, many active learning acquisition functions have been proposed, leaving practitioners with an unclear choice of which to use. Bayesian active learning offers principled objectives with explainable intuition, including Expected Error Reduction (EER), Expected Predictive Information Gain (EPIG), and Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreements (BALD). A key challenge of such methods is the difficulty of extending to the batch setting, leading to either computational challenges (BatchBALD) or dramatic performance drops (top-$B$ selection). In this work, we extend active learning's Bayesian Decision Theory framework to derive Partial Batch Label Sampling (ParBaLS) for the EPIG algorithm. We show experimentally that ParBaLS EPIG gives superior performance for a variety of datasets with different budgets using Bayesian logistic regression on embeddings from large pre-trained models. Our code is available at https://github.com/ADDAPT-ML/ParBaLS.
item.dc:creator: Kangping Hu, Stephen Mussmann

item.title: Stochastic Difference-of-Convex Optimization with Momentum
item.description: arXiv:2510.17503v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the online stochastic difference-of-convex (DC) program $\min_{x \in R^n} F(x) = G(x) - H(x) + r_1(x) - r_2(x)$, which covers sparse learning with nonconvex penalties, robust regression with smooth robust losses, and non-negative positive--unlabeled learning. We propose \emph{momentum-based DCA} (MDCA), which combines a damped DCA step with a momentum estimator for $\nabla H$ and uses a constant per-iteration batch size. With exact solutions of the convex subproblems, MDCA with Polyak momentum uses $\mathcal{O}( \epsilon^{-4})$ stochastic gradients of $H$ to reach $\epsilon$-stationarity, and momentum-based variance reduction (MVR) uses $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3})$ under averaged smoothness, with a single $\mathcal O(\epsilon^{-1})$ warm-up batch in place of the periodic large batches of DCA-PAGE, whose $\epsilon$-dependence it matches. We also introduce a single-loop variant (S-MDCA) that replaces the subproblem solve by one stochastic prox-gradient step; for every fixed smoothing parameter $\gamma$ for which the separately smoothed surrogate $F_\gamma$ is bounded below, it reaches $\epsilon$-stationarity of $F_\gamma$ in $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ iterations, which does not by itself imply stationarity of $F$. A variance--drift trade-off lemma describes how the momentum parameter trades estimator variance against iterate-drift bias in steady-state upper bounds. Guarantees are given for two criteria: the critical-distance measure, and a DCA fixed-point residual that requires no smoothness of $r_2$ and vanishes exactly at DC-critical points; both give the same $\epsilon$-dependence. Experiments on two LIBSVM classification datasets illustrate the methods' behaviour.
item.dc:creator: El Mahdi Chayti, Martin Jaggi

item.title: Deep Jump Gaussian Processes for Surrogate Modeling of High-Dimensional Piecewise Continuous Functions
item.description: arXiv:2510.21974v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce Deep Jump Gaussian Processes (DJGP), a novel method for surrogate modeling of a piecewise continuous function on a high-dimensional domain. DJGP addresses the limitations of conventional Jump Gaussian Processes (JGP) in high-dimensional input spaces by integrating region-specific, locally linear projections with JGP modeling. These projections employ region-dependent matrices to capture local low-dimensional subspace structures, making them well suited to the inherently localized modeling behavior of JGPs, a variant of local Gaussian processes. To control model complexity, we place a Gaussian Process prior on the projection matrices, allowing them to evolve smoothly across the input space. The projected inputs are then modeled with a JGP to capture piecewise continuous relationships with the response. This yields a distinctive two-layer deep learning of GP/JGP. We further develop a scalable variational inference algorithm to jointly learn the projection matrices and JGP hyperparameters. Rigorous theoretical analysis and extensive empirical studies are provided to justify the proposed approach. In particular, we derive an oracle error bound for DJGP and decompose it into four distinct sources of error, which are then linked to practical implications. Experiments on synthetic and benchmark datasets demonstrate that DJGP achieves superior predictive accuracy and more reliable uncertainty quantification compared with existing methods.
item.dc:creator: Yang Xu, Chiwoo Park

item.title: The Optimization Landscape of Carath\'eodory Decomposition of Toeplitz Covariances
item.description: arXiv:2511.01605v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Toeplitz covariance estimation is a classical signal processing problem, yet the geometry of the Gaussian maximum-likelihood objective remains only partially understood. Recent Newton-type, majorization-minimization, and gradient-based methods often solve the nonconvex problem globally with enough samples, but also reveal a difficult computational landscape. We study this phenomenon through an overparameterized Carath\'eodory representation, which parameterizes the covariance by the frequencies and amplitudes of steering vectors. A simple example shows that, for any uniform frequency grid, optimizing only the amplitudes can leave a positive error even in the population setting, which motivates optimizing the frequencies as well. Our main result proves that this nonlinear parameterization adds no stationary points: for any sample covariance, every stationary point with a positive definite covariance gives a stationary point of the Toeplitz maximum-likelihood problem. In the population setting, every such point therefore recovers the true covariance. We also prove that gradient descent converges to the true covariance in the population setting, and to the unique maximum likelihood estimate when the sample covariance is close enough to the true covariance. These results do not require overparameterization. Numerically, overparameterization speeds up gradient descent and gives a more accurate estimate for a fixed number of iterations.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Busbib, Ami Wiesel

item.title: An Infinite BART model
item.description: arXiv:2511.20087v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) is a popular Bayesian ensemble model used in regression and classification analysis. Under this modeling framework, the regression function is approximated by an ensemble of decision trees, interpreted as weak learners. In this work, we propose a generalization of the BART model that has two main features: first, it automatically selects the number of decision trees using the given data; second, the model allows clusters of observations to have different regression functions since each data point can only use a selection of weak learners, instead of all of them. This model generalization is accomplished by including a binary weight matrix in the conditional distribution of the response variable, which activates only a specific subset of decision trees for each observation. Such a matrix is endowed with an Indian Buffet process prior, and sampled within the MCMC sampler, together with the other BART parameters. We then compare the Infinite BART model with the classic one on simulated and real datasets. Specifically, we provide examples illustrating variable importance, partial dependence and causal estimation.
item.dc:creator: Marco Battiston, Yu Luo

item.title: Fully Bayesian Spectral Clustering and Benchmarking with Uncertainty Quantification for Small Area Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2512.15643v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this work, inspired by machine learning techniques, we propose a new Bayesian model for Small Area Estimation (SAE), the Fay-Herriot model with Spectral Clustering (FH-SC). Unlike traditional approaches, clustering in FH-SC is based on spectral clustering algorithms that utilize external covariates, rather than geographical or administrative criteria. A major advantage of the FH-SC model is its flexibility in integrating existing SAE approaches, with or without clustering random effects. To enable benchmarking, we leverage the theoretical framework of posterior projections for constrained Bayesian inference and derive closed form expressions for the new Rao-Blackwell (RB) estimators of the posterior mean under the FH-SC model. Additionally, we introduce a novel measure of uncertainty for the benchmarked estimator, the Conditional Posterior Mean Square Error (CPMSE), which is generalizable to other Bayesian SAE estimators. We conduct model-based and data-based simulation studies to evaluate the frequentist properties of the CPMSE. The proposed methodology is motivated by a real case study involving the estimation of the proportion of households with internet access in the municipalities of Colombia. Finally, we also illustrate the advantages of FH-SC over existing Bayesian and frequentist approaches through our case study.
item.dc:creator: Jairo F\'uquene-Pati\~no

item.title: Measuring all the noises of LLM Evals
item.description: arXiv:2512.21326v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Applying well-established statistical methods effectively to LLM evals requires consideration of model correlations and prediction noises. Leading evals often ignore data noise, have low statistical power, or make unnecessary trade-offs. We define and measure three types of noise: 1) prediction noise from generating different answers on a given question, 2) data noise from sampling questions, and 3) their combined total noise following the law of total variance. To emphasize relative comparisons and gain statistical power, we propose \emph{all-pairs comparison}, which applies paired comparison to all pairs of LLMs and measures all the noise components based on millions of question-level predictions across many evals and settings, revealing clear trends. First, most evals exhibit a characteristic and highly predictable total noise level across all model pairs. Second, paired prediction noise typically exceeds paired data noise, which means reducing prediction noise by averaging can significantly increase statistical power. By measuring all the noises together, we can assess eval results in context and make better empirical decisions.
item.dc:creator: Sida I. Wang

item.title: Signal from Structure: Exploiting Submodular Upper Bounds in Generative Flow Networks
item.description: arXiv:2601.21061v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets; GFNs) are a class of generative models that learn to sample compositional objects proportional to their a priori unknown value, their reward. We focus on the case where the reward has a specified, actionable structure, namely that it is submodular. We show submodularity can be harnessed to retrieve upper bounds on the reward of compositional objects that have not yet been observed. We provide in-depth analyses of the probability of such bounds occurring, as well as how many unobserved compositional objects can be covered by a bound. Following the Optimism in the Face of Uncertainty principle, we then introduce SUBo-GFN , which uses the submodular upper bounds to train a GFN. We show that SUBo-GFN generates orders of magnitude more learning signal than classical GFNs for the same number of queries to the reward function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SUBo-GFN in terms of distribution matching and high-quality candidate generation on graph submodular tasks.
item.dc:creator: Alexandre Larouche, Audrey Durand

item.title: Transfer Denoising of Low-Rank Plus Sparse Matrices under Ambient and Rank Growth
item.description: arXiv:2601.21873v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study transfer learning for low-rank plus sparse matrix denoising when both ambient and latent dimensions grow. A data-rich source task provides subspace information for a higher-dimensional, data-scarce target with a small rank increment and localized sparse edits. We develop an anchored alternating-projection estimator that preserves transferred subspaces while learning target-specific coefficients, additional latent directions, and sparse modifications. We establish deterministic error bounds that separate target noise, representation growth, and source-estimation error, identifying improved rates through small structural increments and reduced noise within inherited subspaces. We further extend it to approximate anchoring quantifies robustness to subspace mismatch. We establish application-specific guarantees for Markov transition matrix estimation from single trajectories with dependent noise and for structured covariance estimation, with the latter analysis provided in the appendix. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over non-transfer baselines on synthetic data and an approximately 45\% reduction in principal-angle error on a NYC taxi transition-estimation task with expanding state spaces.
item.dc:creator: Elynn Chen, Jinhang Chai, Xuyuan Liu, Yujun Yan

item.title: DCD: Decomposition-based Causal Discovery from Autocorrelated and Non-Stationary Temporal Data
item.description: arXiv:2602.01433v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multivariate time series in domains such as finance, climate science, and healthcare often exhibit long-term trends, seasonal patterns, and short-term fluctuations, complicating causal inference under non-stationarity and autocorrelation. Existing causal discovery methods typically operate on raw observations, making them vulnerable to spurious edges and misattributed temporal dependencies. We introduce a decomposition-based causal discovery framework that separates each time series into trend, seasonal, and residual components and performs component-specific causal analysis. Trend components are assessed using stationarity tests, seasonal components using kernel-based dependence measures, and residual components using constraint-based causal discovery. The resulting component-level graphs are integrated into a unified multi-scale causal structure. This approach isolates long- and short-range causal effects, reduces spurious associations, and improves interpretability. Across extensive synthetic benchmarks and real-world climate data, our framework more accurately recovers ground-truth causal structure than state-of-the-art baselines, particularly under strong non-stationarity and temporal autocorrelation.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Hasan Ferdous, Ian Stockwell, Md Osman Gani

item.title: Certified Per-Instance Unlearning Using Individual Sensitivity Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2602.15602v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Certified machine unlearning can be achieved through noise injection, with differential privacy guarantees obtained by calibrating the noise to worst-case sensitivity.
